How to read the diagrams

Boxes are things that exist on disk or in memory. Diamonds are decisions. A copper arrow is the normal path. A red arrow is a refusal — the pipeline stopping on purpose, with a typed error naming the measured number that caused it. Refusals are drawn as prominently as successes because in this system they are the more interesting half.

Part 1

What this is, in plain language

Before any code: what problem exists, who has it, and what this repository does about it. No prior machine-learning knowledge is assumed. Every term is defined the first time it is used.

1.1  The situation

Start with a company that wants an AI assistant for its own business. Not a general chatbot — an assistant that knows their shipments, their equipment, their customers, and that can take real actions on them: look something up, add a note, reroute an order, put a batch on hold.

Building that from nothing takes months. Most of the work is not about the business at all. It is the plumbing: how the assistant decides which action to take, how a risky action gets a human's approval before it runs, how you stop it answering questions it has no business answering, how you record what it did.

Aegis is that plumbing, built once. It is an enterprise AI-agent platform: the routing, the safety rails, the approval gates, the audit trail, the memory, the retrieval of reference documents, the machine-learning spine. All of it is domain-neutral — it does not know or care whether you ship vaccines or repair forklifts.

Words defined
agent
A program built on a large language model that can decide to call functions (“tools”) rather than only producing text. Asking it “which shipments are at risk?” makes it call a lookup tool, read the result, and answer.
domain
The specific business the assistant is for. Cold-chain pharmaceutical logistics is a domain. Industrial equipment maintenance is a different domain.
tool
One named function the agent is allowed to call, with typed arguments and a declared risk tier. “Look up shipment” is low risk. “Quarantine a batch” is high risk and stops for human approval.

1.2  Retargeting Aegis means writing one adapter

Because Aegis is domain-neutral, pointing it at a new business does not mean editing Aegis. It means writing one Python package that Aegis loads: the domain adapter. The adapter is where all the business knowledge lives, and it is the only thing that changes between one deployment and the next.

The adapter is ten pieces. This is a fixed contract — Aegis ships a test suite, aegis.conformance, whose fourteen checks verify that all ten are present and wired correctly.

#PieceFileWhat it declares
1Data schemaschema.pyThe nouns of this world — the entities and their fields. Every other piece uses this vocabulary.
2ML features & targetml_spec.pyWhat is being predicted, from which columns, and the true underlying relationship the data is generated from.
3Synthetic generatorgenerator.pyMakes fake but believable records, labelled using piece 2's relationship.
4Tool definitionstools.pyThe real actions, typed, risk-tiered, and allowed per user type.
5Personaspersonas.pyWho is being served, what data each may see, which tools each may call.
6Promptsprompts.pyWho the assistant is, per persona — plus a platform floor no tenant may edit.
7Memory contractmemory_spec.pyWhat counts as a durable fact worth remembering, and whose memory a conversation touches.
8Agent rosterroster.pyWhich specialist sub-agents exist and which one handles an unmatched question.
9Domain corpuscorpus/Seed documents — policies, runbooks — loaded into the search index.
10Procedural skillsskills/How-to-act playbooks, chosen per question.

Source: templates/adapter/README.md and reference/README.md. Ten pieces map to nine DomainAdapter members — skills/ has none of its own, because it is already named by memory_spec.SKILLS_DIR. The other two members are DOMAIN_ID and DOMAIN_DESCRIPTION, both in __init__.py, which is why the repository elsewhere says eleven members across ten pieces.

1.3  Where the trouble starts

Piece 2 and piece 3 are the machine-learning half of the adapter, and they are where everything quietly goes wrong.

A new deployment has no historical data. Nobody hands you five years of shipment records. So piece 3 generates the data: it invents thousands of plausible records and attaches a label to each one — the thing the model is supposed to learn to predict.

The label has to be a real function of the columns. If it is not — if the generator draws it at random — then there is nothing to learn, and the model that trains on it learns nothing. That is obvious when stated. It is invisible in practice, and here is why:

Trap — the expensive one

Nothing in Aegis catches a noise target. All fourteen conformance checks pass on a frame whose label is drawn from a random number generator. They check the adapter's structure, and a random label is structurally perfect: right column name, right dtype, right bounds. The whole backend test suite passes. The agent test suite passes. ruff passes.

The only native symptom anywhere in the platform is the word distinct=False on the final line of python -m app.ml — read minutes before a demo, at which point the fix is a regenerate-and-retrain cycle you no longer have time for.

Verified in docs/02-domain-adapter-contract.md §6 against aegis/src/aegis/conformance/test_conformance.py: zero references to the generator exist in the conformance suite.

And there is a second, quieter failure in the opposite direction. Suppose the generator does compute the label from the columns, but adds almost no noise. Then the label is very nearly a formula, and a model recovers it almost perfectly. You get a score like R² 0.99, and it looks like a triumph.

It is not. It is a tell. It announces that the data is a toy, and it destroys the one thing that made the system worth trusting — the honest uncertainty estimate. A range calibrated on near-zero errors is a hairline that impresses nobody and informs no decision.

Stated plainly

Aegis's own reference generator does exactly this. It uses a flat noise_scale=4.0 against a latent signal that spreads roughly thirty hours, which lands around R² 0.97–0.98. It is present in the code everyone pattern-matches from. Do not copy it.

Recorded at ISSUES.md issue #15, SESSION.md, and reference/README.md. Flagged as “not our bug, but worth knowing before copying anything from it.”

1.4  What aegis_ml is

aegis_ml is a separate Python package — it is not part of Aegis and it edits nothing inside Aegis. It exists to make the machine-learning half of a domain adapter correct, measured and defensible, and it is built around a single conviction stated in its own source:

Never produce a plausible-looking number that nobody measured. A missing measurement is recorded as missing, because nobody investigates a gap they cannot see.

Concretely, it does eight things:

It does thisWhich means
Proves the data is honestRefuses a label that is noise; shouts about a label that is too easy; measures how realistic the generated frame actually is against a declared band.
Finds a leaking columnDetects a feature that already contains the answer — the one that produces the best score in the lab and the worst behaviour in production.
Searches for the modelRuns four families of automatic model search and ranks every candidate on one shared held-out split, keeping the losers on the record.
Measures uncertaintyTurns a single predicted number into a range with a coverage guarantee that is measured, not asserted.
Looks at segmentsScores every slice of the data separately, because an average hides a collapsed region.
Explains predictionsAttributes each prediction to the columns that drove it, in the domain's own words.
Gates promotionFive criteria, all required, every number recorded — before the served file is replaced.
Watches it afterwardsCompares live data against the frame frozen at training time, and estimates performance before any true answers arrive.

1.5  The analogy that holds

Aegis has a machine-learning spine already: a fitted model, a calibrated range around each prediction, per-prediction attribution, a model card. It is genuinely good, and aegis_ml does not replace it.

That last sentence is the whole integration story. Promotion — putting a new model into service — is replacing the one .joblib file that aegis.ml.get_model() already loads. No new service, no new endpoint, no change inside aegis/.

Why this shape was chosen

Because it makes the factory deletable. If aegis_ml vanished tomorrow, Aegis would keep serving the model it has. Nothing in the request path depends on the factory being present, running, or reachable. A trained artifact never depends on a server being up — that is recorded as architecture decision D4 in finalplan.md.

1.6  How big is it

14subpackages under src/aegis_ml/

7pipeline flows in pipelines/flows.py
323tests collected by pytest

The test count above is what pytest --collect-only -q reports in this checkout today. The repository's own documents disagree with each other on this figure — ISSUES.md line 289 says 323 passed, while SESSION.md, README.md and ISSUES.md line 51 all say 314. This handbook quotes the number it measured and flags the discrepancy rather than choosing between them. See Part 8.

Part 2

Architecture

One map of the whole system, then each layer explained. Then the single decision that shapes everything else: why the machine-learning libraries live in a second Python environment, and what crosses the boundary between them.

The diagram overleaf reads top to bottom. A problem statement enters as prose. It leaves as a file the Aegis platform loads and serves. Everything in between is aegis_ml.

Three things to notice on it. First, the ten adapter pieces at the top are the contract with Aegis — aegis_ml generates and validates two of them (ml_spec.py and generator.py) and leaves the other eight alone. Second, the dashed line down the middle of the venv band is a process boundary: two Python environments that cannot see each other's libraries, with a small JSON document crossing between them. Third, the feedback arrow on the right is what makes this MLOps rather than a training script — live data comes back and is compared against the frame frozen at training time.

2.1  Reading the layers

BandWhat lives thereWhat it is responsible for
1 Inputprose → Brief → MLProblem Turning a sentence into a typed object with no remaining ambiguity. The MLProblem is the single spec three consumers read: the generator, the pipeline, and the adapter itself. Because it is one object, the target's name cannot be spelled two ways.
2 Adapterten Python files The contract with Aegis. aegis_ml generates ml_spec.py and supplies the latent function that generator.py labels rows with. It never edits the other eight.
3 aegis_mlfourteen subpackages All the actual work. Group A decides whether the data is worth training on at all. Group B searches for a model. Group C measures it and explains it. Group D ships it, watches it, and shows it to a human.
4 Environmentstwo .venv directories The heavy libraries cannot be installed next to Aegis. So they are not. See §2.2.
5 Recipeone JSON file The only thing that crosses the boundary. It is a list of estimator class names plus their constructor arguments — version-independent by construction.
6 Spineaegis.ml.model Aegis's own code, unmodified. It rebuilds the ensemble from the recipe, recalibrates the interval, and produces the served object.
7 Artifactone .joblib file The deliverable. Promotion is replacing this file atomically, with the previous one kept so rollback is one command.
Words defined
virtualenv (venv)
An isolated folder holding one Python interpreter and its own copy of every library. Two venvs on the same machine can hold incompatible versions of the same library without interfering.
estimator
One model object with a .fit() and a .predict() — a single gradient-boosted tree ensemble, a ridge regression, and so on.
ensemble
Several estimators whose predictions are averaged. Usually better than any one of them alone.
joblib / pickle
Python's way of writing a live object to a file and reading it back. It only works reliably if both sides have the same library versions — which is exactly why it is never used across the boundary in band 4.
Parquet
A compact, typed file format for tables. Used instead of CSV because it preserves column types exactly.

2.2  The keystone: why there are two environments

This is the decision the rest of the architecture bends around, so it is worth stating precisely.

Aegis's backend has hard version ceilings that come from libraries that have nothing to do with machine learning. Its guardrails package needs pandas below 2.4. Its personally-identifiable-information scanner needs numpy below 2.5. A compiler library called numba is pinned to exactly 0.67.0.

The strongest model-search libraries — AutoGluon, TabPFN, and the PyTorch they sit on — will not install under those ceilings. There is no clever pin that fixes it. So there are two choices: give up the strong models, or run them somewhere else.

2.3  What a Recipe actually is

A Recipe is deliberately unexciting. Here is a real one, from the run stored at registry_store/runs/cold_chain_logistics-20260824T093252907-b2ee26/recipe.json:

{
  "task": "regression",
  "members": [ { "name": "linear", "kind": "RidgeCV", "params": {}, "weight": 1.0 } ],
  "categorical_features": ["carrier_tier","route_class","packaging_type",
                           "origin_region","product_class"],
  "numeric_features":     ["transit_hours","ambient_temp_c","handoff_count",
                           "payload_kg","sensor_gap_minutes"],
  "tier": "baseline",
  "search_seconds": 15.279030084027909,
  "notes": [ "linear reference 'ridge_reference', fitted on 975 rows; the member is wrapped
              in SimpleImputer(median) + StandardScaler ...",
             "Selected on r2 over 326 held-out rows (25% of 1301), seed=11.", ... ]
}

There is no model in there. There is a description of a model. The serving environment reads "kind": "RidgeCV", looks it up in an explicit allowlist of 21 permitted estimator kinds, constructs it with those parameters, and fits it on its own copy of the data.

Why an allowlist and not a dynamic import

A recipe is data produced by another process. Writing getattr(import_module(mod), kind) on a class name that arrived as data is an arbitrary-import primitive — a security problem. But there is a more immediate problem: it succeeds for classes that cannot survive the crossing. AutoGluon's WeightedEnsembleModel imports perfectly well in the trainer environment and is meaningless in the serving one.

So a name that is not in the map is refused with RecipeNotPortableError rather than imported, and that tier's score is reported as an accuracy ceiling — “here is how good this problem could get” — instead of being promoted.

2.4  The 21 portable kinds

Two families, admitted for two different reasons. Verified against src/aegis_ml/automl/recipe.py::PORTABLE_KINDS.

FamilyModuleCountKinds — and why they are allowed across
Tree learners
explained exactly by shap.TreeExplainer in milliseconds, no reference data needed		 xgboost2XGBRegressor, XGBClassifier — the spine's primary member, present in both environments.
sklearn.ensemble6HistGradientBoosting{Regressor,Classifier}, RandomForest{Regressor,Classifier}, ExtraTrees{Regressor,Classifier}.
lightgbm2LGBMRegressor, LGBMClassifier — listed, but importability is checked per member before a search may select it, because LightGBM is not a serving dependency.
Linear learners
explained exactly by shap.LinearExplainer; each is wrapped in SimpleImputer(median) → StandardScaler		 sklearn.linear_model11 Ridge, RidgeCV, LinearRegression, ElasticNet, ElasticNetCV, Lasso, LassoCV, SGDRegressor, LogisticRegression, LogisticRegressionCV, SGDClassifier.
Total21Everything else is refused, including anything AutoGluon or TabPFN produces.
A real decision, with the cost measured

The linear family was added recently, and the reason is instructive. The allowlist used to be trees only, justified by the fact that the spine explained itself with shap.TreeExplainer, which supports trees and nothing else.

But that described a limit of the tooling while deciding a modelling question. In a measured run, the linear reference scored r² 0.7460 — the best score on the board — and was refused promotion in favour of a model that scored 0.7379, purely because the explainer could not explain it. A measured cost of 0.008 r², paid to protect a tool.

The tool was fixed instead: the explainer now dispatches per member (see Part 3, explain), and the allowlist grew to admit what dispatch can now handle. Aegis's own tree path is byte-identical after the patch, and its own suite passed 57 tests before and after.

2.5  One more property worth knowing

Importing aegis_ml.contracts costs pydantic and nothing else. No pandas, no scikit-learn, no torch. There is a test that asserts this in a subprocess.

The reason is practical: Aegis's backend has a light API-schema layer that needs to name these shapes — what a TrainResult looks like, what a GateDecision looks like — without dragging the entire machine-learning stack into the web process. Every heavy import in aegis_ml happens inside the function that needs it, routed through a helper called _require.require().

That helper does one more thing that matters. A missing library raises an error naming the exact command that installs it, rather than being caught and silently routed to a weaker code path. The failure mode it exists to prevent is this: a bare try/except ImportError around a search tier turns “AutoGluon is not installed” into “AutoGluon found nothing better than the baseline” — and the leaderboard in the demo cannot tell those two apart.

contracts

the vocabulary everything else speaks

In one sentence. It defines what a problem looks like, what a result looks like, and what a refusal looks like — as typed Python objects that validate themselves.

Why it exists

Three separate consumers need to agree on the name of the target column: the generator that makes the data, the pipeline that trains on it, and the adapter Aegis loads. If each keeps its own copy of that name, the day they disagree is the day the pipeline reports “no such column” twenty minutes into a run. So there is exactly one object, MLProblem, and everything reads it.

The second reason is import weight. This subpackage imports pydantic and nothing else — no pandas, no scikit-learn — and a test asserts it in a subprocess. That lets Aegis's web layer name these shapes without pulling in the ML stack.

Public API

MLProblemFeatureSpecTargetSpecDTypeTaskType RecipeRecipeMemberCandidateLeaderboard TrainResultSliceMetricGateDecisionDriftReport RegistryEntryRunManifestTierName

Refusals: AegisMLErrorLabelNotLearnableErrorTargetLeakageErrorInsufficientLabelsErrorRecipeNotPortableErrorPromotionRejectedErrorAutoMLTierUnavailableErrorDriftThresholdExceededErrorTrainerVenvMissingError

Also contracts.frames: schema_forvalidate — derive the pandera data contract from the same MLProblem.

The field that carries the whole design

On TrainResult, these two sit next to each other and are never merged:

requested_coverage: float           # the level you ASKED FOR
empirical_coverage: float | None    # MEASURED on held-out rows. None = not measured.

The | None is deliberate. A run that could not measure coverage records None and says why, rather than defaulting to something plausible. Part 7 explains why this distinction is load-bearing.

Worked example

from aegis_ml.contracts import MLProblem, FeatureSpec, TargetSpec

problem = MLProblem(
    domain_id="equipment_maintenance",
    features=[
        FeatureSpec(name="asset_class", dtype="categorical",
                    description="What kind of machine it is",
                    levels=["pump", "conveyor", "press", "chiller"]),
        FeatureSpec(name="runtime_hours", dtype="numeric", unit="h",
                    description="Hours since last overhaul",
                    minimum=0.0, maximum=20000.0),
    ],
    target=TargetSpec(name="repair_hours", task="regression", unit="h",
                      description="Hours of technician time the repair will take",
                      minimum=0.5, maximum=72.0),
    primary_metric="r2",
    requested_coverage=0.9,
)

Put repair_hours in the feature list as well and the object refuses to construct — that is perfect leakage, and it is the one leakage case Aegis itself already catches.

data

is this frame worth training on?

In one sentence. It declares the true relationship the generated labels are built from, splits the rows the same way Aegis splits them, and proves — in seconds — that the label is actually learnable.

Why it exists

Four jobs, each of which, if skipped, produces a believable number instead of an error. An AutoML search over a target that carries no signal costs five minutes to discover what a learnability probe finds in two seconds.

The five modules

ModuleJob
latent.pyThe declared function labels are sampled around, plus the whole realism layer — calibrated noise, unobserved confounders, missingness, boundary label noise — and the two-directional learnability guard. Part 6 is about this module.
splits.pyReproduces aegis.ml.model.train's three-way split exactly, guards the calibration size the conformal interval needs, and refuses to shuffle a time series.
profile.pyDescribes a frame for a machine and for a human.
contract_check.pyRuns schema, learnability and structural checks together and returns one report.
synth.pyThe alternative inbound path: fit SDV to a real CSV and sample more of it.

Public API

assert_learnablemeasure_learnabilityLearnabilityReport LatentModelLatentDriverInteractionConfounder MissingnessRuleRealismConfigLatentCalibration default_latent_modelrealism_reportR2_CEILINGACCURACY_CEILING three_way_splitstratified_splitgrouped_splittime_ordered_split min_calibration_rowsThreeWaySplit profile_framesummarize_columnsummarize_columns checkContractReportColumnAudit synthesizefit_synthesizersamplequality_reportFittedSynthesizer

Why three splits and not two

Most tutorials split data in two: train and test. Aegis splits in three, and this module reproduces that exactly, because the third piece is what makes the uncertainty claim honest.

The calibration set must also be big enough for the confidence level you asked for. A split-conformal interval takes the ceil((n+1)·level)-th smallest calibration error as its half-width. If that rank exceeds n, no such error exists and the requested level is unattainable no matter how good the model is. min_calibration_rows() computes it: 9 rows at 90%, 99 rows at 99% — and refuses before an expensive search rather than at fit time.

Worked example

from aegis_ml.data import assert_learnable, three_way_split

score = assert_learnable(frame, problem)      # raises if the label is noise
split = three_way_split(frame, problem, seed=11)
print(len(split.train), len(split.calibration), len(split.test))
# 1301 326 407

features

encoding, and the column that already knows

In one sentence. One preprocessing path that must exactly mirror Aegis's, one richer path for exploration, and a detector for the feature that secretly contains the answer.

Why it exists — two separate reasons

Reason one: the encoding must not drift. column_transformer() is a deliberate mirror of aegis.ml.model._build_preprocessor — one-hot with handle_unknown="ignore", numeric passthrough, remainder="drop". It has to be, because the recipe crosses a process boundary and is re-fitted by the Aegis spine under its preprocessor, and because SHAP attribution is reconstructed from exactly that column layout. A search that ranks candidates under a different encoding is ranking them on a different problem.

Reason two: leakage. Aegis catches only the perfect case — MLProblem refuses a target that is also a feature. Every subtler form produces the best-looking numbers in the entire pipeline, right up until the model meets a row where the leaking column is not yet populated.

Words defined
one-hot encoding
Turning a categorical column into several 0/1 columns, one per level. route_class with four levels becomes four columns. Models do arithmetic, so text has to become numbers.
handle_unknown="ignore"
If a level appears at prediction time that was never seen in training, encode it as all zeros instead of crashing. This is why every categorical feature must declare its full level set in the spec — an undeclared level silently becomes all-zeros and the model quietly ignores it.
target leakage
A feature that would not actually be available at the moment you need the prediction, because it is a consequence of the answer rather than a cause of it. The test question is: at the moment we make this prediction, do we really know this?

Public API

column_transformerencode_frameskrub_pipeline detect_leakageassert_no_leakageLeakSignal

Worked example

from aegis_ml.features import detect_leakage

for signal in detect_leakage(frame, problem):
    print(signal.feature, signal.score, signal.threshold)
# repair_cost_invoiced 0.994 0.98   <-- the invoice is written AFTER the repair

The detector fits a single-feature model per column and flags any column that predicts the target on its own above settings.leakage_threshold, which defaults to 0.98. A column that good is almost never a genuine predictor.

automl

four tiers, one leaderboard, one portable recipe

In one sentence. It tries several families of model-finding algorithm, scores every candidate on one shared held-out split, keeps the losers on the record, and selects the best one that can cross back into the serving environment.

Why it exists

Choosing a model by hand is guesswork, and choosing one by running four searches with four different splits is worse — the scores are not comparable. So there is one split, one metric, one board. And critically: every tier that does not run leaves a reason string behind, so a leaderboard reader can tell “we chose not to” from “we could not” from “it ran and lost”.

The seven modules

ModuleJob
tiers.pyWhat can run here, and why the rest cannot. Probes availability with importlib.util.find_spec — never by importing, because importing AutoGluon costs seconds and drags torch into memory.
search.pyRuns every available tier, scores every candidate on one held-out split, selects the best portable one.
recipe.pyThe allowlist and both ends of the venv bridge. Rebuilds a recipe into the exact [(name, estimator)] shape Aegis's spine returns.
hpo.pyOptuna refinement of the chosen recipe. TPE + Hyperband, resumable from a SQLite study on disk.
runner.py / _worker.pyThe subprocess bridge into the trainer venv.
strong.pyPersists AutoGluon/TabPFN models with pinned versions so a strong score can actually be called later, not just reported.
_predict_worker.pyLoads a persisted strong model and predicts with it, inside the trainer venv.

              Install with `uv pip install 'aegis-ml[strong]'`, or run the search
              through aegis_ml.automl.runner, which executes it inside the trainer venv."
"tabpfn":    "not importable in this interpreter: tabpfn. Install with ..."

That is the whole point of the reason string. Nobody reading this board can mistake the absence of AutoGluon for AutoGluon having lost.

What Optuna added, measured

Also from that run's recipe notes, verbatim:

"Optuna study 'cold_chain_logistics::spoilage_risk_pct::r2' — 372 complete trials
 (522 total, resumable), TPE + Hyperband, 3-fold CV on 1301 rows, 4.9s this invocation."
"Untuned recipe scored r2=0.7351 on the same folds."
"Tuned recipe scored r2=0.7353 (trial #336), an improvement of 0.0002."
"Members ['RidgeCV'] have no search space defined in aegis_ml.automl.hpo and kept their
 parameters verbatim — they are UNTUNED, not optimally tuned."
Note the last line

An improvement of 0.0002 is honestly reported as an improvement of 0.0002. And a member with no search space is recorded as UNTUNED, not optimally tuned — two very different claims that a less careful system would render identically.

evaluate

every number a promotion decision rests on

In one sentence. It computes the scores, the fold-to-fold spread, the measured coverage, the per-segment breakdown, and the five-criterion verdict that decides whether a model goes into service.

Why it exists

One conviction, stated in the package's own docstring: an aggregate score is not evidence on its own. It hides fold-to-fold instability, so cv reports the standard deviation next to the mean. It hides mis-stated confidence, so calibration keeps requested and measured coverage as two separate fields, always. It hides a collapsed segment, so slices finds it and gate compares the worst one, not the mean.

The metric direction problem

metrics.HIGHER_IS_BETTER exists because every other module here needs a metric's direction before it can say which of two numbers is better. For r2 and accuracy, higher wins. For rmse and log_loss, lower wins. Get it backwards and you promote the worse model without a single suspicious-looking figure anywhere in the record.

The gate never writes >. It asks the registry.

Public API

HIGHER_IS_BETTERhigher_is_betterscoreprimaryregression_metricsclassification_metricsUnknownMetricErrorMetricNotComputedError cross_validatenested_cvresolve_strategyCVReportCVStrategyFoldScoreTemporalShuffleError coveragecoverage_reportcoverage_by_slicecalibration_reportreliability_curveexpected_calibration_errorbrier_scoremean_interval_widthmean_set_sizeCoverageReportCalibrationReportReliabilityBin slice_metricsslice_reportworst_sliceSliceReportSkippedSlice CRITERIAGateConfigevaluate_gatepromote_or_raiseformat_decision

Worked example

from aegis_ml.evaluate import evaluate_gate, format_decision

decision = evaluate_gate(challenger, champion, contract_ok=True, leakage=[])
print(decision.promoted)              # True
print(format_decision(decision))     # the block the CLI prints and the card embeds

Two entry points exist for two callers. A pipeline that wants to record the decision calls evaluate_gate. A pipeline whose very next statement would overwrite the served artifact calls promote_or_raise, so a rejection cannot be stepped over by a caller who forgot to check .promoted.

Part 7 walks all five criteria in full.

explain

why did it say that?

In one sentence. It attributes each prediction to the columns that drove it, picks the right attribution algorithm for the kind of model in hand, and renders the result as artifacts and as sentences the agent can say out loud.

Words defined
SHAP value
A number per feature per prediction saying how much that feature pushed this particular prediction away from the average prediction. Signed: positive pushed it up, negative pushed it down. They add up exactly to the difference between this prediction and the average one, which is what makes them auditable.
partial dependence (PDP)
A curve showing how the prediction changes as one feature is swept across its range, holding everything else as it is. SHAP tells you which features mattered; PDP tells you the shape of how they mattered.
reason code
One SHAP attribution rendered as a sentence in the domain's own words — “risk is high because the carrier tier is economy, despite the short transit time.”

Why it exists — the dispatch

shap is not one algorithm; it is three, and they differ enormously in what they can be pointed at and what they cost. Both single-algorithm answers are wrong in a way that costs something real.

Pipelines get special handling

A linear member on data with missing values must carry its own imputation, so it arrives wrapped in a Pipeline. When the prefix preserves the column count — an imputer, a scaler — the final estimator is explained directly and the attributions still line up one-to-one with the caller's columns, because an affine per-column transform leaves coef_j · (x_j − E[x_j]) unchanged. When the prefix reshapes the columns, the whole pipeline is explained by permutation instead. That check is made against real transformed data, never guessed from the class name.

Public API

model_familybuild_explainershap_valuesExplainerKindExplainerUnavailableError global_importancelocal_explanationrender_shap_html partial_dependence_curvesPDPCurverender_pdp_htmlPartialDependenceUnavailableError build_reason_codesdescribe_prediction_textemit_describe_prediction_source build_cardExtendedModelCardCoverageBlockrender_htmlrender_markdownmeasure_missingness

The rule every renderer follows

An explanation is only useful stated in the domain's own vocabulary. region = 1.0 is the encoding; region = emea is the fact. Every renderer prefers ShapFeature.value_label over value for exactly that reason — and emit_describe_prediction_source generates the adapter's describe_prediction function so the same rule holds in the generated code that reaches the agent.

registry

what ran, what is serving, and the way back

In one sentence. A directory tree that is the single source of truth about every run, plus the atomic file swap that puts a model into service and the one command that undoes it.

Why it exists

Architecture decision D3, in one sentence: the filesystem is the source of truth, and promotion is replacing the one joblib file aegis.ml.get_model() already loads. Everything in the subpackage follows from that. Two optional mirrors exist — MLflow for the UI, SQLAlchemy tables for hosts that already run a database — and both are off by default. With both off, the registry still trains, gates, promotes, rolls back and serves, which is what makes a demo survivable when a server is not.

What one run directory holds

Ten standard artifacts, from registry.store.STANDARD_ARTIFACTS:

FileContents
model.joblibThe fitted model object.
entry.jsonThe whole RegistryEntry: result, gate decision, paths.
recipe.jsonThe portable recipe that produced it.
leaderboard.jsonEvery candidate, including the losers, and every skipped tier's reason.
metrics.jsonThe headline numbers, flat, for a machine.
card.md / card.html / card.jsonThe model card in three renderings.
shap.htmlSelf-contained attribution report.
reference.parquetThe frame frozen at training time. Every later drift number is measured against this.

In practice a real run directory holds more than the ten — the run inspected for this handbook also carries problem.json, split.json, gate_inputs.json, profile.html, drift.json, current.parquet, three manifest*.json lineage records and a visuals/ directory.

Found while writing this

card.json is listed in STANDARD_ARTIFACTS but is never written by any flow. The repository knows — SESSION.md records it under “judgement calls worth revisiting”. It is repeated here because a reader working from the artifact list would otherwise go looking for a file that does not exist.

promote is a module here, not a re-exported function, because the two cannot both own the name. Use from aegis_ml.registry.promote import promote, or the short spelling aegis_ml.promote at the package root.

Worked example

$ aegis-ml registry --limit 3
$ aegis-ml promote --run-id cold_chain_logistics-20260824T093252907-b2ee26
$ aegis-ml rollback --domain-id cold_chain_logistics

current_artifact_info() answers the question a demo actually needs: which model is serving right now? — by hashing the served file and matching it against the registry, not by trusting a status field.

monitor

what the inputs did, and what to do about it

In one sentence. It logs what was predicted, compares today's incoming data against the frame frozen at training time, estimates how the model is probably doing before any true answers arrive, and turns those measurements into an action.

Words defined
drift
The incoming data has changed shape since training. Not necessarily an error — the world moves — but a model trained on last year's mix may be answering this year's questions badly.
reference frame
A copy of the training data, frozen and stored with the run. Drift is always measured against this file, never against a moving average, so the comparison is reproducible months later.
label-free performance estimation
Estimating how well the model is doing before the true answers arrive. If you predict repair time, you learn the truth when the repair finishes — possibly weeks later. This estimates in the meantime.

Why it reports a share of drifted features

Because with a dozen features tested at p<0.05, one of them firing is the expected outcome under no drift at all. A single flagged column is noise; seven out of ten is a signal. So DriftReport.drifted_share is the headline, and the thresholds are settings: drift_share_warn = 0.2, drift_share_block = 0.4.

The naming rule

Every estimated quantity is named estimated_* — estimated_metric_name, estimated_metric_value — so it can never be read as a measurement. That is not a style preference. A number labelled rmse and a number labelled estimated_rmse support completely different decisions.

What “block” means, precisely

A blocking verdict blocks promotion, never serving. Aegis keeps serving the model it has and flags it. Taking a model out of service because its inputs shifted leaves the agent with no prediction at all, which is worse than a flagged one.

Public API

log_predictionlog_prediction_asyncread_loglog_pathcompact_to_parquetfeature_digest drift_reportframe_digestEvidentlySurfaceError estimate_performanceNannyMLSurfaceError evaluate_alertsraise_if_blockingAlertAlertConfigAlertLevel

Worked example — a real drift report

From registry_store/runs/cold_chain_logistics-20260824T093252907-b2ee26/drift.json, measured against a deliberately shifted frame:

FieldValue
n_reference_rows2,034
n_current_rows934
dataset_drifttrue
drifted_share0.70  above the 0.4 block threshold
drifted_featuresambient_temp_c, carrier_tier, handoff_count, product_class, route_class, sensor_gap_minutes, transit_hours — seven of ten
target_drift0.604
prediction_driftnull — not measured, recorded as such
estimated_metric_nameestimated_rmse

Note which columns are not in the list: packaging_type and origin_region were left alone by the shift, and the detector correctly leaves them alone. A drift detector that flags everything is as useless as one that flags nothing.

report

the one page a human opens

In one sentence. It draws the figures for a run from that run's own artifacts and inlines them into a single self-contained HTML page.

Why it exists

Because the decision “do I trust this model?” is made by a person looking at pictures, not by reading JSON. Every run in registry_store/runs/ gets a visuals/ directory, and visuals/index.html is the single file to open.

The rule the whole package is built around

An input that is missing produces a recorded omission, never a drawn zero. A run whose SHAP stage failed and a run whose features genuinely carry no attribution must not produce the same picture.

The figures

PLOT_FILES declares ten figure kinds: prediction_vs_actual, residuals, conformal_coverage, shap_global, slice_performance, leaderboard, realism, feature_distributions, drift_features, forecast.

Nine are produced by a real tabular run. The tenth, forecast, needs the aegis[forecast] extra, which is not installed here — so it is honestly omitted from every real bundle rather than drawn empty. The nine committed at docs/images/ are exactly that set.

Public API

build_bundlebundle_dirload_assetsrecover_splitMissingInputPLOT_FILESCAPTIONSVISUALS_DIRNAME render_indexwrite_indexPALETTETIER_COLOURS

Plot functions in report.plots: prediction_vs_actual, residuals, conformal_coverage, shap_global, slice_performance, leaderboard, realism_panel, feature_distributions, drift_features, forecast_panel, classification_overview, interactive_report — twelve functions behind the ten file slots.

The split-recovery check — worth calling out

recover_split() does not merely reload the held-out rows; it verifies them. Re-scoring the persisted model on the recovered rows must reproduce the registered score exactly. In the measured case it reproduced r2 = 0.722406014223 exactly, and a deliberately wrong seed produced 0.7805 and was rejected. Without that check, a chart could be drawn from the wrong rows and look perfectly plausible.

Worked example

$ aegis-ml visuals --run-id cold_chain_logistics-20260824T093252907-b2ee26 --open

The resulting index.html has zero external references — no CDN, no font request, no script fetch. It is opened from a filesystem path and read offline, and anything fetched would render blank exactly where the report matters.

dashboard

one hub page in front of two premade UIs

In one sentence. It serves a hand-built page that reads the registry and states the verdict, and starts MLflow and Optuna Dashboard pointed at data this package already writes.

Why it exists — three ideas in order

  1. Do not rebuild what already exists. MLflow's run comparison and Optuna Dashboard's parallel-coordinate plot are best-in-class and already installed. This package writes both of their stores as a side effect of doing its actual job — the Optuna study database exists so a search is resumable, not so a dashboard can read it — so pointing them at that data costs a subprocess each, not a frontend.
  2. Own the thing nobody else can show. No off-the-shelf UI knows what a promotion gate is, or that a conformal interval has a requested coverage and a measured one that must be read next to each other. That verdict is the hub's job, and it is the only page here that is hand-built.
  3. Never show a number that was not measured. Every figure the hub renders is read from an artifact in registry_store/. Where the artifact is missing the page says which one and which command writes it. There is no default, no rounded-up estimate and no sample row anywhere in the package.

Public API

hubserverservicestheme — submodules, exposing collectrenderrun_viewDOC_SLOTS build_serverHubServer superviseprobeSupervisorServiceStatefree_port_fromport_in_usemlflow_store_urioptuna_storage_uri stylesheettokens_csstier_colour

Deletable by design

Nothing here is imported by the training, gating, promotion or serving path. The dashboard is a viewer. Deleting this subpackage changes nothing about what the pipelines produce.

Worked example

$ aegis-ml dashboard
# hub on :8000, MLflow on its own port, Optuna Dashboard on its own,
# a browser opened at the hub. --no-mlflow / --no-optuna / --no-browser to opt out.

forecast

time series, and a refusal to shuffle one

In one sentence. A thin pass-through to Aegis's own forecaster, plus extra machine-learning candidates scored on exactly the same windows, plus the backtest that refuses to random-split a series.

Why it exists

Deliberately not a second forecaster. Aegis already has one — Nixtla StatsForecast, conformal intervals, rolling-origin backtest, three typed refusals and no naive-line fallback. Reimplementing it would create two answers to the same question. What this subpackage adds is a fair comparison: would gradient boosting on lagged values have beaten AutoETS? gets a measured answer on the same windows instead of an opinion.

Trap

A time series must never be randomly shuffled before splitting. Aegis's own engine states the rule outright: calibration rows drawn from after the rows the model trained on make the error distribution optimistic and void the coverage guarantee entirely. So backtest.RandomSplitRefusedError and splits.time_ordered_split raise rather than accepting a shuffle=True they would have to ignore.

Public API

forecastto_forecast_runForecastRunForecastCandidateForecastPointSeriesObservation ml_candidates backtestrank_candidatessummariseBacktestSummaryRandomSplitRefusedError

Every name is resolved lazily on first access, so importing aegis_ml.forecast costs pydantic even though the forecasting stack lives behind an optional extra.

Worked example

$ aegis-ml forecast --data series.parquet --label "Repairs opened per day" \
    --ts-column day --value-column repairs --horizon 14 --freq D --level 0.9

The one rule shared by all three modules: the coverage a caller asked for and the coverage the data achieved are never the same field.

serve

how ML finally reaches the agent

In one sentence. Five ready-made tool specifications that drop into a domain's tool registry, giving the agent the ability to predict, explain, test a scenario, forecast and check model health — with no edits inside aegis/.

Why it exists

This is the gap it closes, and it is a real one. Aegis's ML spine has been trustworthy and unreachable: predict_explain has no consumers in the agent path, and describe_prediction — the adapter member that renders a prediction into the plan — has zero consumers across the entire codebase. The platform README describes an ml_predict graph node that does not exist.

The answer is not to add a node. It is to route ML through adapter tools, which are already wired, already gated, already audited and already visible in the console.

The five tools

ToolWhat the agent gets
predict_outcomeA prediction with its calibrated interval.
explain_predictionSigned per-feature attribution — “high because x, despite y”.
whatif_scenarioThe prediction under a modified set of inputs.
forecast_seriesA series forecast with the band the data achieved.
check_model_healthWhich model is serving, its measured coverage, its drift verdict.
The platform rule this respects

ML informs; it never gates. The human approval gate fires on a tool's risk tier. All five of these are LOW risk, read_only=True and destructive=False — asserted, not derived — because a prediction is evidence for a decision, never the decision. In the reference domain this yields nine registered tools: four domain actions plus these five.

Public API

ml_tool_specsML_TOOL_DEFINITIONSML_TOOL_NAMESML_TOOL_RISKMLToolResult predict_outcomeexplain_predictionwhatif_scenarioforecast_seriescheck_model_health build_router

Worked example — the entire integration

# in the domain adapter's tools.py
from aegis_ml.serve import ml_tool_specs
from aegis.core.types import ToolSpec

TOOL_REGISTRY = {..., *ml_tool_specs(ToolSpec, problem=PROBLEM)}
ALLOWLIST = {"maintenance_lead": frozenset({..., *ML_TOOL_NAMES})}

That is the whole thing. Two lines, in the adapter, in the destination repository.

pipelines

seven flows, and no server required

In one sentence. Ordinary Python functions that produce every artifact, with a stage-level lineage record, a content-addressed cache, and an orchestrator that is optional in the strictest sense.

Why it exists

Architecture decision D4: a trained artifact must never depend on a server being up. The flows are plain functions returning typed results. prefect_shim turns them into Prefect flows when Prefect is installed and enabled, and does nothing otherwise. The artifacts are identical either way.

The seven flows

FlowWhat it does
data_flowIngest → schema contract → profile → learnability → realism → leakage → chronology-safe three-way split → frozen reference frame.
train_flowAutoML search → Optuna tune → fit → measure on held-out → slices → SHAP → model card → registry.
eval_flowRe-score a registered run on data it has never seen.
promote_flowBuild the gate decision against the current champion, and promote only if it passes.
drift_flowEvidently drift against the frozen reference, plus a NannyML label-free performance estimate.
forecast_flowA series forecast with its achieved coverage.
full_flowThe end-to-end bundle a demo is given.
Documentation defect found

The module docstring of src/aegis_ml/pipelines/flows.py opens with “Six flows, in the order a domain moves through them” and then lists seven, with forecast_flow and full_flow sharing one bullet. There are seven @flow-decorated functions in the file. README.md names only four. Verified by import: data_flow, train_flow, eval_flow, promote_flow, drift_flow, forecast_flow, full_flow.

What a manifest is, and why it is not a log

Each flow leaves a RunManifest: one row per stage with its duration, row counts, measured metrics, cache key and — on failure — the exception attributed to the stage that raised it. That is the difference between a log and a lineage record, and it is what makes a crashed run resumable rather than merely re-runnable.

Four properties that hold across every flow

Every number is measuredNo branch anywhere produces a metric without a fit. A stage that cannot measure records None and says why.
Stages are content-addressedThe expensive stage (the search) is keyed on the frame digest plus its own configuration. A re-run after a crash reuses it; a re-run over changed data cannot, because the digest is part of the key.
Failure is attributedThe manifest names the stage, the exception type and the message. Only reporting stages are optional, and an optional failure is recorded as degraded, not hidden.
The data is assumed hardA held-out R² in the 0.45–0.80 band is the target, not a disappointment.

resume_from=run_id adopts a previous run's recipe and refuses if that run's dataset digest differs — resuming onto different data would silently attribute one dataset's search to another's.

Public API

data_flowtrain_floweval_flowpromote_flowdrift_flowforecast_flowfull_flow DataBundleREALISM_R2_BANDREALISM_ACCURACY_BANDrealism_band_forframe_digest StageGraphStageSpecStageCachestagenew_manifestwrite_manifestrender_summary flowtaskprefect_active

Flow-level refusals: FrameSourceMissingError, InSampleEvaluationError, ResumeMismatchError.

export

portable, with its limits stated first

In one sentence. It converts the fitted point predictor to ONNX and proves the conversion by round-tripping it — and says loudly what does not survive.

Why it exists, and what it is not

An ONNX export is the point predictor only. The conformal interval and the SHAP attributions do not survive the conversion. An ONNX-served prediction has no coverage guarantee and cannot explain itself.

It is a portability and verification artefact — a file another runtime can score, plus a measured round-trip difference proving it computes the same function — not an alternative serving path for Aegis, which already answers in under a millisecond with the interval.

Two measured limits, neither fixed

LimitMeasured evidence
Missing values break itThe same RandomForest showed 2.4e-06 max absolute difference on complete rows and 17.7 on rows containing NaNs. The synthetic data deliberately carries ~4% missing-at-random values, so this is not a corner case.
One family will not convertHistGradientBoosting does not convert on skl2onnx 1.20 with the current onnx.

Both are accepted limitations, recorded in ISSUES.md, and export is off by default.

Public API

to_onnxvalidate_roundtripregister_convertersDEFAULT_TOLERANCE

Worked example

$ aegis-ml export --run-id <run> --out model.onnx --validate
Part 4

The pipeline, as a flowchart

Four flows, thirty-one stages, and every way the pipeline can stop on purpose. The refusals are drawn as prominently as the successes, because they are the interesting half — a system that only ever succeeds has not been tested.

Read the chart overleaf down the left column first, then across to the right. Copper is the normal path. Red is a refusal: the pipeline stopping deliberately, with a typed error carrying the measured number that caused it. The two diamonds are the two places where the pipeline genuinely decides something rather than merely doing something — the learnability guard, and the promotion gate.

4.1  Each stage: in, out, and what stops it

data_flow — stages 1 to 8

StageGoes in / comes outWhat makes it stop
1 Ingesta path or an adapter module → a DataFrameFrameSourceMissingError — neither --data nor a resolvable adapter was given.
2 Schema contractframe + MLProblem → pass/fail per columnNothing raises here, but a failure sets contract_ok=False, which fails gate criterion 3 later. Checks dtypes, ranges, null policy, and categorical level sets.
3 Profileframe → JSON summary + optional HTMLOptional stage. A failure is recorded as degraded in the manifest and appended to TrainResult.notes — loud, just not fatal.
4 Learnabilityframe → LearnabilityReportLabelNotLearnableError below the floor. Above the ceiling sets suspiciously_easy and logs a warning; with strict_ceiling=True it escalates to TargetLeakageError or AegisMLError. Also InsufficientLabelsError below 60 labelled rows.
5 Realismframe + latent model → evidence dictReports rather than refuses. Compares achieved against the oracle and the analytic ceiling, and against the declared band.
6 Leakageframe → list of LeakSignalAny single feature predicting the target above leakage_threshold (0.98) is flagged. Findings fail gate criterion 5.
7 Splitframe → ThreeWaySplitInsufficientLabelsError when the calibration set is too small for the requested coverage. TemporalShuffleError if something tries to shuffle a series.
8 Freezeframe → reference.parquet + SHA-256 digestCannot fail meaningfully. This file is what every future drift number is measured against.

train_flow — stages 9 to 19

StageGoes in / comes outWhat makes it stop
9 Resolve tiersrequested tiers → (to_run, skipped)Never stops. Even an unknown tier name is skipped with a reason, which is how a typo in --tier becomes visible instead of silent.
10 Searchtrain rows → every candidate scored on one shared holdoutCached on the frame digest. TrainerVenvMissingError if a strong tier was demanded and .venv-ml is absent. A hung child is killed on timeout — never returned as a partial result.
11 Selectleaderboard → the best portable recipeRecipeNotPortableError if a demanded member is not in the 21-kind allowlist. A strong tier's win is kept as an accuracy ceiling, not promoted.
12 Tunerecipe → refined parametersOptional (--no-hpo). Members with no declared search space are recorded as UNTUNED, not as optimally tuned.
13 Fittrain rows → a fitted modelAny fit error is attributed to this stage by name in the manifest.
14 Calibratecalibration rows → interval half-widthThe rows here are disjoint from both train and test. This is the whole basis of the coverage claim.
15 Scoretest rows → metric_value, empirical_coverageInSampleEvaluationError if a caller tries to score on rows the model saw. eval_flow can waive this with --allow-in-sample, and then labels the result IN-SAMPLE.
16 Slicestest rows → list[SliceMetric]Every level of every categorical, plus quartiles of every numeric. Segments too small to score are recorded as SkippedSlice, not dropped.
17 SHAPmodel + background → attributionsOptional reporting stage. Dispatches tree / linear / permutation. A failure is degraded.
18 Card & visualseverything → card + nine figures + index.htmlOptional. A missing input produces a recorded omission, never a drawn zero.
19 Registereverything → a run directory + index entryAtomic writes. The index is rebuildable from the directories with reindex(), so a corrupt index is not a lost run.

promote_flow and drift_flow — stages 20 to 31

StageGoes in / comes outWhat makes it stop
20 Load championdomain id → the incumbent TrainResult or NoneNone is normal for a first model, and criteria 1 and 4 then pass trivially — and say so in the reason string.
21 The gatechallenger + champion → GateDecisionPromotionRejectedError from promote_or_raise. Every criterion is evaluated even after one fails — short-circuiting would hide the second problem, which is the one that reappears after you fix the first.
22 Swaprun's model → ml_spine.joblibAtomic. Write to a temporary path, then rename.
23–24 Recordprevious artifact kept; stage set to productioncurrent_artifact_info() answers “what is serving?” by hashing the file, not by trusting the stage field.
25 Logeach prediction → an append-only logWithout this there is no current frame and every drift number is computed on data assembled by hand for a screenshot.
26–27 Comparecurrent vs reference.parquet → per-feature testsEvidentlySurfaceError if the drift library's own surface changed.
28 Thresholddrifted share → verdict0.20 warns, 0.40 blocks. Configurable.
29 Estimatecurrent frame → estimated_rmseNannyMLSurfaceError. Refuses below MIN_CHUNK_ROWS / MIN_REFERENCE_LABELS rather than estimating from too little.
30–31 Actverdict → alertsDriftThresholdExceededError from raise_if_blocking. Blocks promotion, never serving.

4.2  The four AutoML tiers, and where each one runs

Stage 10 is the expensive one, and it is the only stage that may leave the process it started in. Which tiers are available depends on which interpreter is asking — the same call to available_tiers() gives a different answer in the two environments, and the answer is reported rather than acted on quietly.

TabPFN needs one-time setup, and it is not optional

From TabPFN 8.x the package imports fine with no model weights on disk, then raises TabPFNLicenseError inside .fit() — after the search has already spent its budget and someone is watching a progress line. So availability is probed rather than assumed: the tier is reported unavailable unless TABPFN_TOKEN is set or a checkpoint is already cached locally.

Setup needs a browser and a network: register at ux.priorlabs.ai, accept the licence, copy the key, export TABPFN_TOKEN=..., run once to cache the weights. Do this before the day you need it.

Licence, verbatim from TABPFN_LICENSE_NOTICE: TabPFN-2.5 weights are distributed under the Prior Labs License — research and evaluation use are permitted, commercial and production use are NOT. This tier's score is reported as an accuracy ceiling for evaluation purposes only. Set AEGIS_ML_ENABLE_TABPFN=0 to switch it off entirely. That notice is a module constant rather than a docstring precisely because it has to be copied into data — into Recipe.notes, into Candidate.detail, into the model card. A licence condition that exists only in a docstring travels nowhere.

Part 5

A new problem statement, start to finish

One paragraph of client prose, followed all the way to a model an agent can call. The worked example is deliberately not the cold-chain reference domain, so what you see is the method rather than a copy.

About the numbers in this part

The commands below are real and the file shapes are real. The example domain (“equipment repair time”) has not been built, so no measured number is claimed for it. Where output is shown, it is either the literal format the tool prints, or the reference domain's genuine measured output clearly labelled as such. Your numbers will differ — that is the point.

5.0  The journey, in one picture

  1. The problem statement, as the client wrote it

    This is the raw input. One paragraph, no structure, several unstated assumptions:

    “We run maintenance for a few hundred industrial machines across four plants — pumps, conveyors, presses and chillers. When a fault ticket comes in, the planner has to promise the production line a return-to-service time, and they are guessing. If they promise four hours and it takes twelve, the line schedules around a lie. We want something that estimates how many hours of technician time a repair will actually take, tells the planner why it thinks so, and flags when it is not confident. Planners should be able to try scenarios — ‘what if we send two technicians?’ The system should also be able to look up a ticket, add a note to it, reassign it to a different crew, and take a machine out of service for inspection.”

    Notice what is not in there: no column names, no data types, no units, no idea what makes a repair long. That is normal. Step 2 removes every one of those decisions.

  2. What the Domain Brief extracts from it

    prompts/00-intake.md defines this step exactly. Its instruction to the agent: “You are not writing code in this task. You are removing every remaining decision.” The output is one file, DOMAIN_BRIEF.md, in a fixed template — same headings, same order, same table columns, because every later prompt parses it by heading.

    Its rules, verbatim from the prompt, are the interesting part:

    #Rule
    1Fill every field. If the statement does not say, decide and mark the row [assumed]. An unfilled field becomes an invented value three prompts later, and inconsistently.
    2Every identifier must be a valid Python identifier, snake_case, unique within its section.
    3Every categorical feature must declare its full level set — the encoder uses handle_unknown="ignore", so an undeclared level silently encodes to all zeros.
    4The target must not appear in the feature list. That is perfect leakage.
    5No feature may be a deterministic function of the target. Ask of each: “at the moment we make this prediction, do we actually know this?”
    68–12 features. Fewer makes a thin SHAP story; more makes a slow search and a cluttered chart.
    7At least one HIGH-risk tool — a domain with no gated action cannot demonstrate the human approval gate.
    8Use the client's language for anything a human reads. These are sentences someone reads on screen.
    9Avoid every word in the shipped domain's quarantined vocabulary, so conformance check #14 is exercised for real.

    Applied to the paragraph above, the Brief's key sections come out like this:

    Brief sectionExtracted
    1 Identitydomain_id = equipment_maintenance. Title: Industrial Equipment Maintenance. DOMAIN_DESCRIPTION is a 40–80 word paragraph — and it is a control input, not metadata: Aegis wires it straight in as allowed_topics. A vague description is a loose rail.
    2 EntitiesMachine, FaultTicket, Technician, Plant, PartRequest. Enums become StrEnums whose .value strings become the categorical levels.
    3 The supervised problemTarget repair_hours, regression, unit h, bounds 0.5–72.0, primary metric r2, requested coverage 0.9. Plain-English meaning: how many hours of technician time this repair will consume. Decision it supports: what the planner promises the line.
    4 FeaturesTen rows — see step 3. One or two are marked irrelevant on purpose.
    5 Latent drivers“This is the most important section in the Brief.” The generator computes label = latent_fn(features) + noise, and this table is latent_fn. Step 4 below.
    Trap — rule 5 in practice

    The tempting feature for this domain is parts_cost_invoiced. It is strongly related to repair time and it is sitting right there in the data. It is also leakage: the invoice is written after the repair finishes, so at the moment the planner needs the estimate, that column is empty. A model trained with it in scores beautifully and is useless.

    aegis_ml.features.detect_leakage catches this in step 5 — but only if it made it into the spec. Rule 5 is the cheaper place to catch it.

  3. The resulting MLProblem and ml_spec.py

    Ten features, five categorical and five numeric, two of them deliberately given no influence on the target:

    #FeaturedtypeDriver?Levels / range — and why it is here
    1asset_classcategoricalyespump, conveyor, press, chiller — a press strip-down is not a pump reseal.
    2fault_categorycategoricalyesbearing, seal, electrical, control_software, structural.
    3access_ratingcategoricalyesopen, confined, overhead, permit_required — a permit space doubles the clock before anyone touches a spanner.
    4plant_sitecategoricalnonorth, south, east, west — deliberately irrelevant.
    5shift_startedcategoricalyesday, evening, night — night shift waits longer for parts.
    6runtime_hoursnumericyes (saturating)0–20,000 h since overhaul. Wear rises then plateaus, so the shape is tanh.
    7fault_severitynumericyes (linear)1–5, the planner's triage score.
    8parts_on_handnumericyes (linear)0–12 of the parts the fault code implies. Fewer means waiting.
    9machine_mass_kgnumericno50–9,000 kg — deliberately irrelevant.
    10last_service_gap_daysnumeric, nullableyes (log1p)0–900 days. Missing on machines with no service record — and the missingness is not random, which is the point.
    Why two features are given no driver on purpose

    Because a model that correctly assigns plant_site and machine_mass_kg near-zero attribution is a far better demonstration than one where every column is load-bearing. It is the difference between “the model uses everything” and “the model found the signal and ignored the noise”. In the reference domain those two features land at 1.7% and 1.5% of total attribution — visible on the SHAP chart in Part 3 as the two hatched bars.

    The corresponding MLProblem, which aegis-ml init writes as JSON and ml_spec.py mirrors as Python:

    $ aegis-ml init --domain-id equipment_maintenance \
    --target repair_hours --task regression --unit h \
    --out problem.json --templates ./adapter
    # adapter/ml_spec.py — piece 2 of 10 (sketch; the real file also carries
# the generator's latent function, the tool argument models and describe_prediction)

DOMAIN_ID = "equipment_maintenance"

FEATURES = [
    FeatureSpec(name="asset_class", dtype="categorical",
                levels=["pump", "conveyor", "press", "chiller"],
                description="What kind of machine the ticket is against"),
    # ... eight more ...
    FeatureSpec(name="last_service_gap_days", dtype="numeric", unit="d",
                minimum=0.0, maximum=900.0, nullable=True,
                description="Days since the last scheduled service, where recorded"),
]
FEATURE_NAMES = [f.name for f in FEATURES]

TARGET = TargetSpec(name="repair_hours", task="regression", unit="h",
                    minimum=0.5, maximum=72.0,
                    description="Technician-hours the repair will consume")

PROBLEM = MLProblem(domain_id=DOMAIN_ID, features=FEATURES, target=TARGET,
                    primary_metric="r2", requested_coverage=0.9)

IRRELEVANT_FEATURES = ("plant_site", "machine_mass_kg")


def training_frame(num_records: int = 1200) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One column per FEATURE_NAMES, plus repair_hours."""
    ...

    The keyword is num_records, not num_tickets — deliberately domain-neutral, because the core Protocol names it and a Protocol spelling it after one domain's nouns would force every future domain to call its rows by that name.

  4. Designing the latent function — the part that decides everything

    This is where a domain succeeds or fails. The generator does not invent labels; it computes them from a declared function of the features and then adds a carefully sized amount of noise. In code that is a LatentModel.

    from aegis_ml.data import (LatentModel, LatentDriver, Interaction,
                            Confounder, MissingnessRule, RealismConfig)

latent = LatentModel(
    intercept=6.0,                       # a baseline repair, in hours
    drivers=[
        LatentDriver(feature="runtime_hours",        weight=5.0,  transform="tanh"),
        LatentDriver(feature="fault_severity",       weight=3.4,  transform="identity"),
        LatentDriver(feature="parts_on_hand",        weight=-1.8, transform="identity"),
        LatentDriver(feature="last_service_gap_days", weight=2.1,  transform="log1p"),
        LatentDriver(feature="access_rating",        weight=4.2),   # per-level
        LatentDriver(feature="asset_class",          weight=3.1),
        LatentDriver(feature="fault_category",       weight=2.7),
        LatentDriver(feature="shift_started",        weight=1.4),
        # plant_site and machine_mass_kg appear NOWHERE. That is the point.
    ],
    interactions=[
        Interaction(features=("access_rating", "asset_class"), weight=1.6),
    ],
    confounders=[
        Confounder(name="undocumented_corrosion",    weight=1.0),
        Confounder(name="technician_crew_experience", weight=0.8),
    ],
    missingness=[
        MissingnessRule(feature="last_service_gap_days",
                        depends_on="asset_class", rate=0.04),
    ],
    realism=RealismConfig(
        target_r2=0.72,                              # the CEILING, not a prediction
        heteroscedastic_feature="runtime_hours",      # noise widens with wear
    ),
)
    The calibrated-noise formula

    You do not pick the noise size by hand. You declare the R² you want to be achievable and the noise size is computed from the signal's own variance:

    σ = sqrt( var_signal × (1 − target_r²) / target_r² )

    The derivation is one line. If the signal has variance V and you add unexplained variance U, the best achievable R² is V/(V+U). Hitting target_r2 = r therefore needs U = V(1−r)/r. That budget is then split between the confounders and the pure noise, so an unobserved confounder is not free extra noise on top of the number you asked for.

    Why this matters more than it looks. Hand-tuned constants make the achievable R² an accident of whatever numbers happened to be typed. Calibrating it makes the ceiling a declared property you can check afterwards. Part 6 walks the whole variance budget.

    Setting target_r2 is a judgement, and it is not the score you will get

    target_r2 is the ceiling an oracle — a model that knew the generating function exactly — would hit. A real model on a few thousand rows lands below it. In the reference domain, TARGET_R2 = 0.74 produces a measured held-out R² between 0.62 and 0.71 across sample sizes and seeds. Calibrating the ceiling to 0.65 instead would put the achieved score near 0.48 — below the realism band's floor.

  5. aegis-ml contract — what it proves

    $ aegis-ml contract --problem problem.json --data frame.parquet

    One command, three proofs, in seconds — before anything expensive runs:

    It provesBy doing whatAnd refuses with
    The frame matches the specBuilds a pandera schema from the same MLProblem the adapter uses, and validates dtypes, ranges, null policy and categorical level sets.A recorded contract failure → gate criterion 3 fails later.
    No column already knows the answerFits a single-feature model per column and flags anything predicting the target alone above 0.98.TargetLeakageError, naming the column and its score.
    The label is learnableFits a HistGradientBoosting probe on a train split and scores it on held-out rows.LabelNotLearnableError below the floor; suspiciously_easy above the ceiling.

    Two things to know about that third check. The probe is a gradient-boosting model, not a linear one, deliberately: a linear probe would answer “no signal” for a target built from interactions and saturating transforms — a false alarm that sends a domain author back to rewrite a generator that was correct. And for classification the floor is raised to the majority-class rate plus 0.02, because a 95/5 target hands a constant predictor 0.95 accuracy while learning nothing.

    Known issue: ISSUES.md #19 records that the installed aegis-ml console script cannot import a working-directory-relative adapter module — --adapter reference.problem fails in an importlib traceback. python -m aegis_ml.cli works. Use --problem with a JSON path, or the module form, until that is fixed.

  6. aegis-ml train — what comes back

    $ aegis-ml train --problem problem.json --data frame.parquet \
    --tier baseline --tier flaml --time-budget 120 --seed 11 --hpo

    Add --trainer-venv to send the search into .venv-ml and pick up the AutoGluon and TabPFN tiers. Add --full to promote and drift-check in the same invocation.

    What comes back is a TrainResult and a run directory. The result carries, among other fields:

    FieldMeaning
    metric_valueMEASURED on the held-out test split. Never on rows the model saw.
    requested_coverage / empirical_coverageTwo fields, always. The second may be None.
    training_size / calibration_size / test_sizeThe three-way split, so a reader can judge whether the numbers mean anything.
    dataset_digestSHA-256 of the frame. This is what makes the stage cache safe and resume_from honest.
    recipe / leaderboardWhat won, and everything that lost, with reasons for every tier that did not run.
    slicesEvery level of every categorical, plus numeric quartiles.
    notesHuman sentences: how the interval was calibrated, what the learnability probe scored, what was left untuned.

    Here are two genuine notes entries from the reference domain's real run, quoted to show the register these are written in:

    "split conformal on 326 disjoint calibration residuals; half-width 13.94
 at the 0.9049 quantile"
"learnability probe scored 0.672 against the realism band [0.45, 0.80]"

    $ aegis-ml promote --run-id equipment_maintenance-<timestamp>-<hash>
